issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner in this 34-year-old male unless there is unreported trauma content involving pregnancy, childbirth, or infants. The other trigger items point toward sexualized/interpersonal threat and hospital-associated reminders, making this item the clearest trauma-incongruent outlier.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeated lock-checking is more suggestive of fear of external intrusion/burglary than trauma-specific coping with partner physical abuse, and it is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The other maladaptive strategies reflect interpersonal avoidance and affect suppression, whereas this item introduces a different safety concern.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item duplicates compulsive checking behavior rather than describing a perceived current threat state, and it implies fear of break-in/external danger that is not otherwise supported by the trauma narrative, appraisals, or memory content. In combination with the matching maladaptive strategy item, it forms an internally coherent pair but one that is poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

vignette: Kofi's eyes scan the room with a mixture of habit and unease, his gaze darting towards the door before returning to the present moment. It's been two years since he escaped the abusive relationship that left him with physical scars and a deep-seated sense of vulnerability. As a parole officer, Kofi is no stranger to tense situations, but it's not the rough streets or hardened offenders that unsettle him – it's the quiet moments, like this one, when memories creep in. The smell of antiseptic wafts through his mind, transporting him back to the hospital where he was treated for his injuries. He can almost taste the metallic tang of blood and disinfectant, a sensory echo that makes his stomach churn. Kofi's body tenses, a reflexive response honed from months of being on edge around his former partner. His eyes narrow, and for an instant, he's back in that cramped apartment, waiting for the next blow to fall. Kofi pushes away the memories, a coping mechanism he's developed over time. He can't afford to let his emotions get the better of him – not when he has to keep his cool on the job. Positive feelings are suspect, too; they make him feel vulnerable, like he's letting his guard down. So he focuses on the concrete tasks at hand, avoiding eye contact with colleagues and sidestepping conflicts whenever possible. The constant tension in his body is a reminder that danger lurks around every corner. Kofi finds himself scanning the streets for potential threats – men who look too big, too aggressive, or just plain suspicious. His gaze lingers on strangers' hands, wondering if they're hiding something. He watches people closely, searching for tells, for any sign that they might be a threat. When memories do resurface, Kofi hears the sound of shattering glass and muffled shouting – auditory echoes from that fateful night. The taste of blood returns, too, a bitter reminder of his own vulnerability. Time warps in those moments; the past feels present, and he's right back there, reliving the fear. It's this sense of perpetual danger that gnaws at Kofi's soul. He can't shake the feeling that his life has been irreparably damaged by the trauma. What happened to him was deeply unjust – the beatings, the belittling, the constant gaslighting. No one held his partner accountable; no one made things right. It's a festering wound that refuses to heal. Some days, Kofi wonders if it's all worth it – this fragile existence, this constant vigilance. Is life just about existing in a state of perpetual hypervigilance? He longs for the carefree days when he could walk down the street without scanning for threats or flinch at every loud noise. Kofi's relationship with his new partner is strained; she can't understand why he pushes her away, why intimacy feels like a minefield. His job performance has suffered, too – the constant tension and distraction make it hard to focus on his work. He knows he needs help but fears being vulnerable all over again. That's what brought him here, seeking therapy in the hopes of finding some semblance of peace.
